bioIntro: Ryne works with teens, individuals, couples, and families who are seeking to feel understood in a world that often feels confusing, invalidating, or uncertain.
bioBody:
Ryne works with teens, individuals, couples, and families who are seeking to feel understood in a world that often feels confusing, invalidating, or uncertain—especially when it comes to questions like whether they’re “doing this whole life thing right.” Many of the clients Ryne supports are part of historically marginalized communities and are navigating the intersections of multiple identities. They often arrive feeling disconnected from others, burned out, or struggling with anxiety and depression as a result of long-standing pressure to adapt to systems that were not built with them in mind.


Ryne approaches therapy from a relational and trauma-informed lens, with particular attention to how patterns develop over time and how early experiences shape the way we view ourselves, our relationships, and the world around us. Rather than focusing on quick fixes, Ryne’s work emphasizes building a more compassionate relationship with oneself—supporting clients in moving toward acceptance, understanding, and non-judgmental awareness of who they are.


Sessions are collaborative and conversational, balancing reflection with gentle structure and practical support when helpful. Clients often describe working with Ryne as thoughtful, grounding, and genuine.


As a queer and neurodivergent therapist, Ryne brings both professional training and lived experience into the room, and is deeply committed to creating a space that is affirming, curious, and responsive to each client’s unique way of being. Ryne welcomes clients who are new to therapy as well as those returning after past experiences that may not have felt fully supportive.

bioBody:
Cheryl works with adults and couples who are navigating the effects of trauma, chronic stress, identity-related concerns, and relationship challenges. Many of the clients she supports come to therapy when recurring emotional patterns, disconnection, or relationship difficulties begin to impact their sense of stability or well-being.

Her work is grounded in a relational, trauma-informed approach that pays close attention to how early experiences, attachment patterns, and nervous system responses shape the way people relate to themselves and others. Rather than focusing on quick fixes, Cheryl views therapy as a collaborative and reflective process focused on building insight, emotional awareness, and more integrated ways of understanding one’s experiences.

Cheryl has a particular interest in working with neurodivergent adults and LGBTQ+ individuals, including those exploring gender, sexuality, or identity. She is committed to providing an affirming, flexible therapeutic space that honors different ways of thinking, processing, and communicating.

In sessions, Cheryl balances structure with openness and curiosity, adapting the work to each client’s needs and goals. Clients often describe her style as steady, thoughtful, and grounding. She welcomes both individuals and couples who are new to therapy as well as those returning after past experiences that may not have felt fully supportive.

bioBody:
Mary works with teens and adults who often feel out of place in spaces that weren’t built with their identities in mind. Many of her clients are LGBTQIA+, neurodivergent, and/or navigating the complexities of cultural and systemic expectations. If you’re feeling overwhelmed by daily pressures, questioning your identity, or exhausted from trying to fit into a world that doesn't always "get it," you’ll find a space here where you don’t have to explain or justify your experiences. A space where you can show up as you are.

Because you know yourself best, Mary’s role is to sit beside you, offering support and guidance while you choose the direction that feels right for you. Her role is to sit in the passenger seat, supporting you as you choose what direction you want to go, rather than telling you what turns you should take. Sessions are conversational and flexible, creating a supportive space to sort through what’s on your mind rather than feeling like a “traditional” therapy session. Many clients appreciate this open-ended style as it often feels easier to build trust, find a sense of safety, and work through challenges at a pace that feels comfortable and natural.

A core part of this work is the shift from masking to authenticity. So much energy is often spent hiding parts of ourselves to survive or keep the peace. Here, you are invited to drop the performance. The goal is to look at what it means to live authentically; not by following a rigid plan, but by slowly unlearning the expectations that have been placed on you and discovering what actually feels right.

As a queer, Filipino-American, and neurodivergent therapist (AuDHD), Mary brings lived experience and a commitment to social justice into the room. She understands that many struggles stem from trying to function in systems that weren't designed for you. This perspective shapes a practice that is affirming and non-judgmental, where therapy is adapted to fit your way of thinking and being. You don’t need to have the "right words" or clear goals to begin; curiosity and openness are enough.
